title: ACCA LW - Corporate and Business Law
content_provenance: Original practice items authored from the ACCA LW syllabus study guide (English law variant). Not a capture of past exam questions.

items.domain: Essential Elements of the Legal System
items.stem: A company wants to identify which of the following is a primary source of law in England and Wales that a court must apply.
options: An Act of Parliament passed using the correct procedure
A leading textbook written by an academic lawyer
A newspaper report summarising a recent court decision
A speech delivered in Parliament during a debate
items.explanation: Primary legislation, meaning Acts of Parliament, is a mandatory source that courts must apply, whereas textbooks, media reports and parliamentary speeches are not binding sources of law. Hansard may occasionally be consulted to interpret an ambiguous statute but is not itself a source of law.
items.reference: ACCA LW Syllabus Study Guide - Essential Elements of the Legal System

items.domain: Essential Elements of the Legal System
items.stem: A judge deciding a case in a lower court is bound by a rule of law contained in an earlier decision of a higher court. Which part of that earlier judgment creates the binding precedent?
options: The headnote prepared by the law reporter
The ratio decidendi
The obiter dicta
The dissenting judgment
items.explanation: The ratio decidendi is the legal principle on which the decision rests and is the binding part of a judgment. Obiter dicta are remarks made in passing, a dissent is the view of a judge who disagrees with the majority, and the headnote is only the reporter's summary and carries no authority.
items.reference: ACCA LW Syllabus Study Guide - Essential Elements of the Legal System

items.domain: Essential Elements of the Legal System
items.stem: A party who loses a civil case in the High Court wishes to appeal the decision. To which court is such an appeal normally made?
options: The Supreme Court
The Magistrates' Court
The Court of Appeal (Civil Division)
The Crown Court
items.explanation: Civil appeals from the High Court normally go to the Court of Appeal (Civil Division), which sits above the High Court in the hierarchy. The Crown Court hears serious criminal cases, the Supreme Court is the final appellate court, and the Magistrates' Court is a court of first instance for minor matters.
items.reference: ACCA LW Syllabus Study Guide - Essential Elements of the Legal System

items.domain: Essential Elements of the Legal System
items.stem: A government minister makes detailed regulations using powers that Parliament conferred in a parent Act. Which term describes this type of law?
options: Primary legislation
Case law
European Union law
Delegated legislation
items.explanation: Delegated legislation, also called secondary legislation, is law made by a body such as a minister under authority granted by an enabling Act. It is not primary legislation because the parent Act is the primary source, and it is distinct from judge-made case law.
items.reference: ACCA LW Syllabus Study Guide - Essential Elements of the Legal System

items.domain: Essential Elements of the Legal System
items.stem: When interpreting an ambiguous statute a judge decides to apply the literal rule. Which approach does this require the judge to take?
options: Give the words their ordinary, dictionary meaning even if the result seems odd
Choose the meaning that best achieves the purpose of the statute
Read the words so as to avoid an absurd or unjust outcome
Consult a dictionary only when the words used are technical terms
items.explanation: The literal rule requires words to be read in their ordinary and natural meaning, even where that produces an awkward result. The mischief rule looks to the problem the statute was passed to remedy, and the golden rule allows a modification only to avoid absurdity, so those approaches are not the literal rule.
items.reference: ACCA LW Syllabus Study Guide - Essential Elements of the Legal System

items.domain: Essential Elements of the Legal System
items.stem: Two businesses want their commercial dispute resolved privately, with a decision imposed by a neutral third party after a hearing. Which method of dispute resolution provides a decision that is binding on the parties?
options: Negotiation
Arbitration
Mediation
Conciliation
items.explanation: Arbitration produces a binding decision, called an award, which can normally be enforced like a court judgment but is reached privately. Mediation and conciliation are facilitative processes in which the parties retain control, and negotiation involves only the parties themselves, so none of these imposes a decision.
items.reference: ACCA LW Syllabus Study Guide - Essential Elements of the Legal System

items.domain: Essential Elements of the Legal System
items.stem: A local authority makes a decision that appears to go beyond the powers that statute granted to it. Which court procedure allows the lawfulness of that decision to be challenged?
options: A private prosecution
Committing the authority for contempt of court
Judicial review
An appeal on the merits of the decision
items.explanation: Judicial review asks the Administrative Court to examine whether a public body acted within its legal powers and followed proper procedure. It concerns the legality of the decision rather than its merits, and it is distinct from an ordinary appeal, a prosecution or contempt proceedings.
items.reference: ACCA LW Syllabus Study Guide - Essential Elements of the Legal System

items.domain: Essential Elements of the Legal System
items.stem: A person is being sued in a civil court for breach of a contractual duty. Which standard of proof must the claimant satisfy?
options: Beyond reasonable doubt
The criminal standard of certainty
No standard of proof is required in civil cases
The balance of probabilities
items.explanation: In civil proceedings the claimant must prove the case on the balance of probabilities, meaning the claim is more likely than not. Beyond reasonable doubt is the higher criminal standard, and some evidential burden always applies in civil litigation.
items.reference: ACCA LW Syllabus Study Guide - Essential Elements of the Legal System

items.domain: The Law of Obligations
items.stem: A shopkeeper places goods on a shelf with a price tag on each item, and a customer takes an item to the till and offers to pay the marked price. In legal terms, what is the display of the goods on the shelf?
options: An invitation to treat
An offer to sell
An acceptance of the customer's offer
A binding collateral contract
items.explanation: Displaying goods on a shelf is an invitation to treat, an invitation for customers to make offers. The contract is formed only when the customer offers to buy and the shopkeeper accepts at the till, so the shopkeeper is not obliged to sell.
items.reference: ACCA LW Syllabus Study Guide - The Law of Obligations

items.domain: The Law of Obligations
items.stem: A seller posts a letter of acceptance to a buyer in circumstances where the post was a reasonable means of acceptance. When does the acceptance normally take effect?
options: When the buyer replies confirming receipt
When the letter of acceptance is posted
When the buyer receives the letter
When the buyer reads the letter
items.explanation: Under the postal rule, acceptance is complete when a properly addressed letter is posted, provided the post is a reasonable method. The rule does not apply where the offer requires actual communication, and it does not depend on receipt or reading by the offeror.
items.reference: ACCA LW Syllabus Study Guide - The Law of Obligations

items.domain: The Law of Obligations
items.stem: An employer promises to pay an employee an extra sum for work that the employee had already completed before the promise was made. Is the employer's promise enforceable?
options: Yes, because the promise was made in writing
No, because consideration must be adequate in value
No, because past consideration is not good consideration
Yes, because the employee had already performed the work
items.explanation: Past consideration is generally not valid consideration because the act was not given in return for the promise. Consideration must be sufficient, meaning it has some value, but it need not be adequate, so inadequacy of value is not the correct reason here.
items.reference: ACCA LW Syllabus Study Guide - The Law of Obligations

items.domain: The Law of Obligations
items.stem: Two friends make an informal arrangement to share a lottery ticket, expecting no legal consequences. If one refuses to share the winnings, which presumption applies to their arrangement?
options: There is always an intention to create legal relations
The arrangement is automatically a binding commercial contract
The arrangement is void because it concerns gambling
There is no intention to create legal relations in a social arrangement
items.explanation: In social and domestic arrangements the courts presume the parties did not intend to create legal relations, so such agreements are generally not enforceable. The opposite presumption applies in commercial dealings, where an intention to be legally bound is assumed.
items.reference: ACCA LW Syllabus Study Guide - The Law of Obligations

items.domain: The Law of Obligations
items.stem: A and B make a contract in which B promises to pay a sum of money to C, a stranger to the contract. Under the traditional doctrine of privity, what right does C have to enforce this promise against B?
options: C cannot enforce the promise because C provided no consideration and is not a party
C can enforce the promise as a third party beneficiary in every case
C can enforce the promise because B intended C to benefit
C can enforce the promise only if C sues A instead of B
items.explanation: At common law only a party who provided consideration may enforce a contract, so a third party named to receive a benefit cannot normally sue. The Contracts (Rights of Third Parties) Act 1999 created limited exceptions, but the traditional privity rule still denies C an automatic right to enforce.
items.reference: ACCA LW Syllabus Study Guide - The Law of Obligations

items.domain: The Law of Obligations
items.stem: During negotiations a seller tells a buyer that a van has been driven 20,000 miles when the seller knows it has done 80,000 miles. What type of misrepresentation is this?
options: A mere puff with no legal effect
Fraudulent misrepresentation
Innocent misrepresentation
Negligent misrepresentation
items.explanation: A statement made with knowledge that it is false, or without belief in its truth, is a fraudulent misrepresentation. Innocent misrepresentation applies where the maker reasonably believed the statement true, and negligent misrepresentation applies where the maker had no reasonable grounds for belief, so a statement known to be false is more than mere puffery.
items.reference: ACCA LW Syllabus Study Guide - The Law of Obligations

items.domain: The Law of Obligations
items.stem: A dry cleaner displays a prominent sign at the counter limiting liability for damage to clothing, and a customer leaves a jacket after reading the sign. Is the limitation clause likely to be incorporated into the contract?
options: No, because such clauses can never be incorporated by notice
Yes, but only if the customer read the sign aloud
Yes, because reasonable notice was given before the contract was made
No, because the customer did not sign the sign
items.explanation: A term can be incorporated by reasonable notice given before or at the time of contracting, and a prominent counter sign generally meets that test. A signature is one method of incorporation but not the only one, so the absence of a signature and the customer's subjective reading do not prevent incorporation.
items.reference: ACCA LW Syllabus Study Guide - The Law of Obligations

items.domain: The Law of Obligations
items.stem: A business tries to exclude all liability for death caused by its own negligence in a written contract with another business. What is the effect of the Unfair Contract Terms Act 1977 on such a clause?
options: The clause is valid because businesses can agree anything
The clause is valid if it is written in capital letters
The clause is void only if the other party is a consumer
The exclusion of liability for death caused by negligence is void
items.explanation: The Unfair Contract Terms Act 1977 makes void any term excluding liability for death or personal injury caused by negligence, even between businesses. Such a clause cannot be relied on, and making it prominent in the document does not cure it.
items.reference: ACCA LW Syllabus Study Guide - The Law of Obligations

items.domain: The Law of Obligations
items.stem: A hall is hired for a concert but it is destroyed by fire before the date, making performance impossible through no fault of either party. Which doctrine may discharge the contract?
options: The doctrine of frustration
The doctrine of restraint of trade
The doctrine of promissory estoppel
The doctrine of privity
items.explanation: Frustration discharges a contract when an unforeseen event beyond the parties' control makes performance impossible or radically different. Restraint of trade concerns unreasonable restrictions, promissory estoppel concerns reliance on a promise, and privity concerns who may enforce a contract.
items.reference: ACCA LW Syllabus Study Guide - The Law of Obligations

items.domain: The Law of Obligations
items.stem: A carrier delays delivering a mill shaft, and the mill loses profits. Under Hadley v Baxendale, when are lost profits recoverable as damages for breach?
options: Never, because consequential loss is always too remote
When the loss arises naturally from the breach or was in the contemplation of both parties when they contracted
Whenever the claimant can show that some loss has occurred
Only when the loss can be proved with absolute certainty
items.explanation: Hadley v Baxendale limits recoverable damages to losses arising naturally from the breach or those reasonably contemplated by both parties at the time of contracting. This is the remoteness test, so not every loss is recoverable and consequential loss is not automatically excluded.
items.reference: ACCA LW Syllabus Study Guide - The Law of Obligations

items.domain: The Law of Obligations
items.stem: A court asks whether a defendant owed a duty of care in a novel negligence situation. Under the Caparo test, which three elements must be satisfied?
options: Offer, acceptance and consideration
Duty, breach and a signed written agreement
Foreseeability of damage, proximity between the parties, and that it is fair, just and reasonable to impose a duty
Intention, causation and quantifiable loss
items.explanation: The Caparo test requires foreseeability of harm, a relationship of proximity, and that imposing a duty is fair, just and reasonable. Offer, acceptance and consideration belong to contract formation, and negligence does not require intention or a written agreement.
items.reference: ACCA LW Syllabus Study Guide - The Law of Obligations

items.domain: The Law of Obligations
items.stem: A junior electrician undertakes work that an experienced electrician would do to a particular standard. What standard of care does the law of negligence apply to the junior electrician?
options: The standard of an ordinary untrained member of the public
The standard the junior electrician personally believes is adequate
The standard of the most highly qualified expert available
The standard of a reasonably competent electrician performing that work
items.explanation: The standard of care is that of the reasonable person with the relevant skill, so a professional is judged against a reasonably competent member of that profession. It is neither the lay standard, the defendant's own subjective view, nor an idealised expert standard set unreasonably high.
items.reference: ACCA LW Syllabus Study Guide - The Law of Obligations

items.domain: The Law of Obligations
items.stem: A defendant injures a claimant, and before the injury can heal a completely independent and unforeseeable act by a third party causes further harm. What is the usual effect of this independent act on the defendant's liability for the further harm?
options: It may break the chain of causation, so the defendant is not liable for the further harm
It has no effect, so the defendant is always liable for all later harm
It makes the claimant automatically liable for the third party's act
It transfers liability to the third party for the original injury as well
items.explanation: A new, independent and unforeseeable intervening act, sometimes called a novus actus interveniens, can break the chain of causation and cut off the defendant's liability for later harm. The defendant remains liable for the original injury but is not answerable for every subsequent event.
items.reference: ACCA LW Syllabus Study Guide - The Law of Obligations

items.domain: The Law of Obligations
items.stem: In negligence, which test determines whether the type of damage suffered by the claimant is too remote to be recovered?
options: Whether the damage occurred within one year of the breach
Whether the type of damage was reasonably foreseeable
Whether the defendant intended the precise damage
Whether the claimant was insured against the damage
items.explanation: Following the Wagon Mound cases, a defendant is liable only for damage of a type that was reasonably foreseeable at the time of the breach. Precise foresight of the extent, insurance arrangements and an arbitrary time limit are not the governing tests.
items.reference: ACCA LW Syllabus Study Guide - The Law of Obligations

items.domain: The Law of Obligations
items.stem: A delivery driver employed by a supermarket negligently injures a pedestrian while making deliveries during working hours. On what basis is the supermarket likely to be liable?
options: No liability, because only the driver can ever be sued
Strict liability, because delivery work is inherently dangerous
Vicarious liability, because the tort was committed by an employee in the course of employment
Direct liability, because the supermarket personally drove the van
items.explanation: An employer is vicariously liable for torts committed by an employee acting in the course of employment, even without fault by the employer. The employer did not personally commit the tort, the driver may also be liable, and this is not a case of strict liability for an inherently dangerous activity.
items.reference: ACCA LW Syllabus Study Guide - The Law of Obligations

items.domain: The Law of Obligations
items.stem: A customer of a business reasonably relies on a manager's apparent authority to make a contract, even though the manager had been forbidden to do so internally. Is the principal bound?
options: No, because the manager had no actual authority
No, because internal instructions always bind third parties
Yes, but only if the customer had read the principal's internal rules
Yes, because the manager had apparent authority on which the customer reasonably relied
items.explanation: A principal can be bound by an agent's apparent or ostensible authority where a third party reasonably relies on the appearance of authority created by the principal. A secret internal restriction does not defeat apparent authority, and third parties are not expected to inspect internal rules.
items.reference: ACCA LW Syllabus Study Guide - The Law of Obligations

items.domain: Employment Law
items.stem: A business wants to determine whether a worker is an employee or an independent contractor. Which factor is most relevant to this distinction?
options: The degree of control the business exercises over how the work is performed
The age of the worker
The length of the worker's surname
Whether the worker owns a car
items.explanation: The control test, and in modern practice the multiple or economic reality tests, focus on how much control the business has over the manner and method of the work. Age, surname and car ownership are irrelevant to the legal distinction.
items.reference: ACCA LW Syllabus Study Guide - Employment Law

items.domain: Employment Law
items.stem: A new employee starts work under a contract of employment. Under the Employment Rights Act 1996, by when must the employer usually provide a written statement of the main terms?
options: Within seven years of starting work
On or before the first day of employment
Within twelve months of starting work
Only when the employee asks for it
items.explanation: Since April 2020 most employees and workers must receive a written statement of particulars on or before their first day, whereas the older rule allowed two months. It is a legal duty and does not depend on the employee making a request.
items.reference: ACCA LW Syllabus Study Guide - Employment Law

items.domain: Employment Law
items.stem: An employee with two years of continuous service is dismissed without a fair reason. Which claim is most likely available to the employee?
options: A claim for breach of the Human Rights Act 1998
No claim, because two years is too short
Unfair dismissal
Wrongful dismissal for the manner of the dismissal only
items.explanation: Two years of continuous service is generally the qualifying period for an ordinary unfair dismissal claim under the Employment Rights Act 1996. Wrongful dismissal concerns breach of the contract, such as inadequate notice, and is a separate claim rather than the primary one here.
items.reference: ACCA LW Syllabus Study Guide - Employment Law

items.domain: Employment Law
items.stem: An employer dismisses an employee because the employee took part in lawful trade union activities. How is such a dismissal classified?
options: Fair, because the employer gave notice
Wrongful but not unfair
A redundancy dismissal
Automatically unfair
items.explanation: Dismissal for certain prohibited reasons, including taking part in lawful trade union activities, is automatically unfair and does not require the normal two-year qualifying period. Giving notice does not make it fair, and it is not a genuine redundancy.
items.reference: ACCA LW Syllabus Study Guide - Employment Law

items.domain: Employment Law
items.stem: An employer closes a particular workplace and dismisses the staff there because the need for that work has ceased. For what reason are the employees being dismissed?
options: Redundancy
Misconduct
Capability
Statutory illegality
items.explanation: Redundancy arises where the employer's need for employees to do work of a particular kind has ceased or diminished, for example because a workplace closes. Misconduct and capability are separate potentially fair reasons, and statutory illegality concerns a contract that cannot lawfully be performed.
items.reference: ACCA LW Syllabus Study Guide - Employment Law

items.domain: Employment Law
items.stem: An employer refuses to interview a suitably qualified candidate solely because of the candidate's religion. Which type of discrimination under the Equality Act 2010 is this?
options: Harassment
Direct discrimination
Indirect discrimination
Victimisation
items.explanation: Direct discrimination occurs where a person is treated less favourably because of a protected characteristic such as religion. Indirect discrimination arises from a neutral provision, criterion or practice, victimisation follows a protected act, and harassment concerns unwanted conduct.
items.reference: ACCA LW Syllabus Study Guide - Employment Law

items.domain: Employment Law
items.stem: A contract of employment contains no express notice term, and the employee has worked for six years. Under the Employment Rights Act 1996, what is the statutory minimum notice the employer must give?
options: Twelve weeks
Twenty-four weeks
Six weeks
One week
items.explanation: Where the contract is silent, the statutory minimum notice from an employer is one week for each year of continuous service, up to a maximum of twelve weeks, so six years gives six weeks. One week corresponds to the employee's own minimum, and the maximum is twelve weeks, not twenty-four.
items.reference: ACCA LW Syllabus Study Guide - Employment Law

items.domain: Employment Law
items.stem: Which duty does an employer generally owe to employees under the Health and Safety at Work etc. Act 1974?
options: To guarantee that no employee is ever injured at work
To insure every employee against all possible loss
To provide a written safety policy only to senior managers
To ensure, so far as is reasonably practicable, the health, safety and welfare of employees at work
items.explanation: The Act places a duty on employers to ensure, so far as is reasonably practicable, the health, safety and welfare of their employees. It is not an absolute guarantee, does not require insuring every possible loss, and any written safety policy must be available to all employees, not just senior managers.
items.reference: ACCA LW Syllabus Study Guide - Employment Law

items.domain: The Formation and Constitution of Business Organisations
items.stem: Two accountants carry on a business in common with a view of profit without forming a company. Under the Partnership Act 1890, what is their relationship?
options: A partnership
A limited liability partnership
A private limited company
A sole proprietorship
items.explanation: The Partnership Act 1890 defines a partnership as the relation which subsists between persons carrying on a business in common with a view of profit. A limited liability partnership and a company both require registration, and a sole proprietorship involves only one owner.
items.reference: ACCA LW Syllabus Study Guide - The Formation and Constitution of Business Organisations

items.domain: The Formation and Constitution of Business Organisations
items.stem: An ordinary partnership operating under the Partnership Act 1890 incurs a trading debt. How are the partners liable for that debt?
options: Only if the creditor first sues the partnership as a company
Jointly and severally, with each partner's personal assets at risk
Not at all, because the partnership has separate legal personality
Only up to the amount each partner has invested
items.explanation: Partners in an ordinary partnership are jointly and severally liable for the firm's debts, so their personal assets can be used to satisfy them. The ordinary partnership has no separate legal personality, and liability is not limited to the capital contributed.
items.reference: ACCA LW Syllabus Study Guide - The Formation and Constitution of Business Organisations

items.domain: The Formation and Constitution of Business Organisations
items.stem: A group of professionals wants a business form that gives them limited liability but allows flexible internal management. Which form best meets these aims?
options: A company limited by guarantee
A sole proprietorship
A limited liability partnership
An ordinary partnership
items.explanation: A limited liability partnership, formed under the Limited Liability Partnerships Act 2000, is a body corporate with separate legal personality and gives its members limited liability while permitting flexible internal arrangements. An ordinary partnership lacks limited liability, and a sole proprietorship has only one owner.
items.reference: ACCA LW Syllabus Study Guide - The Formation and Constitution of Business Organisations

items.domain: The Formation and Constitution of Business Organisations
items.stem: A shareholder owns almost all the shares in a registered company that trades successfully. If the company incurs debts, what is the usual position regarding the shareholder's personal liability?
options: The shareholder is always personally liable for all company debts
The shareholder is liable only because they own most of the shares
The shareholder is liable because a company cannot own property
The shareholder is not personally liable because the company is a separate legal person
items.explanation: Following Salomon v Salomon, a registered company is a separate legal person distinct from its shareholders, so shareholders are generally not liable for its debts. A majority holding does not itself create personal liability, and there are only limited exceptions such as fraud or personal guarantees.
items.reference: ACCA LW Syllabus Study Guide - The Formation and Constitution of Business Organisations

items.domain: The Formation and Constitution of Business Organisations
items.stem: A company is used as a mere sham by its owner to commit fraud on creditors. Which principle may allow the court to disregard the company's separate personality?
options: Lifting the corporate veil
The doctrine of ultra vires
The doctrine of frustration
The rule in Rylands v Fletcher
items.explanation: Courts may lift or pierce the corporate veil in exceptional cases where the company is used as a device or sham to evade legal obligations or commit fraud. Ultra vires concerns acts beyond a company's powers, frustration discharges contracts, and Rylands v Fletcher concerns strict liability for escapes.
items.reference: ACCA LW Syllabus Study Guide - The Formation and Constitution of Business Organisations

items.domain: The Formation and Constitution of Business Organisations
items.stem: A company wants to offer its shares to the general public and be listed on a recognised investment exchange. Which type of company must it normally be?
options: A company limited by guarantee
A public limited company
A private limited company
An ordinary partnership
items.explanation: A public limited company may offer its shares to the public and can be listed on a recognised investment exchange, subject to minimum share capital requirements. A private company cannot offer shares to the public, a partnership is not a company, and a guarantee company usually has no share capital.
items.reference: ACCA LW Syllabus Study Guide - The Formation and Constitution of Business Organisations

items.domain: The Formation and Constitution of Business Organisations
items.stem: A company wishes to change an internal rule that governs how the company is run. Which document would normally need to be amended to change that rule?
options: The certificate of incorporation
The share register
The articles of association
The memorandum of association
items.explanation: The articles of association contain the company's internal rules on matters such as directors' powers and shareholder meetings, so they are the document to amend. The memorandum records the subscribers' intention to form the company, the certificate proves incorporation, and the share register records holdings.
items.reference: ACCA LW Syllabus Study Guide - The Formation and Constitution of Business Organisations

items.domain: The Formation and Constitution of Business Organisations
items.stem: A director makes a decision that is intended to promote the long-term success of the company for the benefit of its members as a whole. Which statutory duty is the director performing?
options: The duty to avoid conflicts of interest
The duty not to accept benefits from third parties
The duty to exercise independent judgment
The duty to promote the success of the company
items.explanation: Section 172 of the Companies Act 2006 requires a director to act in the way the director considers, in good faith, would most likely promote the success of the company for the benefit of its members as a whole. Avoiding conflicts, refusing third-party benefits and acting independently are separate, though related, duties.
items.reference: ACCA LW Syllabus Study Guide - The Formation and Constitution of Business Organisations

items.domain: The Formation and Constitution of Business Organisations
items.stem: A non-executive director fails to attend board meetings and does not read the board papers, leading to a poor decision. Which duty has the director most likely breached?
options: The duty to exercise reasonable care, skill and diligence
The duty to promote the success of the company only
The duty to declare an interest in a proposed transaction
The duty to act within the company's constitution
items.explanation: Section 174 of the Companies Act 2006 requires a director to exercise the care, skill and diligence that would be exercised by a reasonably diligent person with the director's knowledge and experience. Failing to prepare or attend goes to that standard, while the other duties address different obligations.
items.reference: ACCA LW Syllabus Study Guide - The Formation and Constitution of Business Organisations

items.domain: The Formation and Constitution of Business Organisations
items.stem: A company needs shareholder approval to change its articles of association. What type of resolution is normally required under the Companies Act 2006?
options: A written resolution of the directors only
A special resolution
An ordinary resolution
A board resolution of the directors
items.explanation: Amending the articles requires a special resolution passed by at least 75 percent of the votes cast. An ordinary resolution needs only a simple majority, and the decision is for the shareholders rather than the board alone.
items.reference: ACCA LW Syllabus Study Guide - The Formation and Constitution of Business Organisations

items.domain: Capital and the Financing of Companies and Management
items.stem: A company allots new shares and must decide how to price them. Which statement about the nominal value of a share is correct?
options: A share may be issued at a discount but not at a premium
The nominal value changes with the market price each day
A share must have a fixed nominal value and cannot be issued at a discount to it
A share has no nominal value at all
items.explanation: Under the Companies Act 2006 shares must have a fixed nominal value, and a company may not issue shares at a discount to nominal value, although it may issue at a premium. The nominal value is fixed at issue and does not fluctuate with the market price.
items.reference: ACCA LW Syllabus Study Guide - Capital and the Financing of Companies and Management

items.domain: Capital and the Financing of Companies and Management
items.stem: A company borrows money from a bank and grants the bank a charge over its factory. Which type of charge gives the bank a claim on a specific, identifiable asset?
options: A floating charge
A share pledge
A share option
A fixed charge
items.explanation: A fixed charge attaches to a specific, identifiable asset such as a factory, whereas a floating charge hovers over a class of assets that changes in the ordinary course of business. A share pledge or share option is not a charge over a factory.
items.reference: ACCA LW Syllabus Study Guide - Capital and the Financing of Companies and Management

items.domain: Capital and the Financing of Companies and Management
items.stem: A company creates a charge over its assets in favour of a lender. Under the Companies Act 2006, why does the lender want the charge registered at Companies House?
options: An unregistered charge is void against a liquidator, administrator or creditor
Registration increases the rate of interest payable on the loan
Registration transfers ownership of the charged asset to the lender
Registration is required only for floating charges over inventory
items.explanation: Registration gives public notice of the charge, and if it is not registered within the required period it is void against a liquidator, administrator or creditor, although the debt itself remains valid. Registration does not transfer ownership or change the interest rate.
items.reference: ACCA LW Syllabus Study Guide - Capital and the Financing of Companies and Management

items.domain: Capital and the Financing of Companies and Management
items.stem: A company with accumulated losses wants to pay a dividend to its shareholders. From what fund may a company lawfully make a distribution?
options: Any cash balance shown in the bank account
Distributable profits available for the purpose
The company's share capital at any time
The proceeds of a loan taken out to fund the dividend
items.explanation: A company may make a distribution only out of profits available for the purpose, which are accumulated realised profits less accumulated realised losses. Share capital must generally be maintained and cannot simply be returned to shareholders, and the source is not determined by the bank balance.
items.reference: ACCA LW Syllabus Study Guide - Capital and the Financing of Companies and Management

items.domain: Capital and the Financing of Companies and Management
items.stem: A private company proposes to allot new shares for cash. Which right normally gives existing shareholders the first opportunity to subscribe for the new shares?
options: The right of set-off
The right of reversion
Pre-emption rights
The right of subrogation
items.explanation: Pre-emption rights, under the Companies Act 2006, generally require a company issuing shares for cash to offer them first to existing shareholders in proportion to their holdings. Subrogation, set-off and reversion are unrelated legal concepts.

items.domain: Capital and the Financing of Companies and Management
items.stem: A company in financial difficulty is placed into administration. What is the primary objective of an administrator?
options: To punish the directors for the company's failure
To distribute the company's assets to shareholders first
To wind the company up immediately in every case
To rescue the company as a going concern, if that is reasonably practicable
items.explanation: The primary objective of an administrator under the Insolvency Act 1986 is to rescue the company as a going concern, if that is reasonably practicable. If rescue is not possible, the administrator seeks a better result for creditors than winding up, and punishing directors or paying shareholders first is not the objective.

items.domain: Capital and the Financing of Companies and Management
items.stem: A director continues to trade a company after the point at which the director knew, or ought to have concluded, that there was no reasonable prospect of avoiding insolvent liquidation. Which liability may arise?
options: Wrongful trading under the Insolvency Act 1986
Fraudulent trading only
Breach of the duty to declare an interest in a proposed transaction
No liability, because trading on is always permitted
items.explanation: Wrongful trading under section 214 of the Insolvency Act 1986 can make a director personally liable to contribute to the company's assets for continuing to trade when there was no reasonable prospect of avoiding insolvent liquidation. Fraudulent trading requires actual intent to defraud, and trading on is not automatically permitted.
items.reference: ACCA LW Syllabus Study Guide - Capital and the Financing of Companies and Management

items.domain: Capital and the Financing of Companies and Management
items.stem: A director knowingly makes false statements to suppliers to obtain credit for a company that is already insolvent, intending that they will not be paid. Which liability best describes this conduct?
options: Lawful commercial negotiation
Fraudulent trading
Innocent misrepresentation
A technical breach of the articles of association
items.explanation: Fraudulent trading under the Insolvency Act 1986 involves carrying on business with intent to defraud creditors, and it can lead to personal liability and even criminal sanctions. Innocent misrepresentation involves no knowledge of falsity, articles breaches are internal, and deliberate deception is not lawful negotiation.
